detail.longDescription: arXiv:2611.24823v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Deep brain stimulation (DBS) effectively treats motor symptoms of Parkinson's disease (PD), but it is unclear whether it changes fine hand movements in the same way for every patient. We analyzed 35 sessions of 19 patients with PD from a multi-center cohort performing the CopyDraw task, a drawing task designed to overcome the subjectivity and limited granularity of clinical assessments. Besides standard kinematics (mean velocity, acceleration, jerk, and drawing accuracy), we derived higher distributional moments and non-linear complexity measures, for 38 features in total. DBS effects were quantified with linear mixed models at the group level and with residualized regression and a random-effects meta-analysis per session. The DBS state was decoded per session with regularized linear discriminant analysis to compare feature sets as behavioral labels for deriving physiomarkers for adaptive DBS (aDBS). DBS modulated all 38 features at the group level, most strongly velocity-related features. However, for every feature, the between-subject variability of the DBS effect exceeded the group-level effect. Only one feature, the detrended fluctuation analysis of the distance to the template, showed a significant mean effect across sessions, and it is not a standard kinematic feature. In six sessions without any significant modulation of standard features, complexity measures were modulated instead. For decoding, standard features alone were the best choice in ten of 35 sessions, but combining all 38 features yielded the highest average area under the ROC curve (0.700 vs. 0.677), with the largest gains in sessions that were hard to decode from standard features. DBS effects on hand-motor behavior are individual. Deriving neural markers for aDBS from behavior therefore requires session-specific analyses with individualized features beyond standard kinematics and group-level effects.
